headline: This law gave eligible low-power TV stations a one-year window to apply to the FCC for Class A licenses, which come with stronger broadcast rights.
what_it_does: For one year, low-power television stations that meet certain requirements can apply to the Federal Communications Commission for a Class A license. To qualify, a station must serve a media market with a limited number of TV households, broadcast a minimum number of hours, and meet other conditions. A Class A license gives the station primary status for its spectrum, so it is not displaced if the FCC reallocates that spectrum to another user, while typical low-power stations have only secondary status.

who_it_affects.group: Operators of eligible low-power television stations
who_it_affects.how: They may apply for Class A licenses during the one-year window if they meet the market, broadcast-hour, and other requirements, gaining primary spectrum status if approved.

who_it_affects.group: Other low-power television stations that do not qualify
who_it_affects.how: They remain under the existing secondary-status rules and may still be displaced if the FCC reallocates their spectrum.
The agency must receive and process Class A license applications from eligible stations during the one-year period.

when_it_takes_effect: Enacted January 5, 2023; the application window lasts one year, but the summary does not state its exact start date.
